utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Could you call the case, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am John Ackerman. I am here with Marela Jevtovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good afternoon to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'm Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic, representing General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Yes. I understand there is a problem, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is or may be. We received a message this morning from the VWS that Mr. Draganovic was very unwell last night. He apparently has a heart condition, and I imagine it was the result of testifying about these events -- had to be taken to a doctor this morning. I was given that information and spoke to Defence counsel and asked if they would agree to Mr. Draganovic being seen not by me but by an investigator from the team. They gave me verbal agreement. Because the witness was testifying, I needed the Trial Chamber's authority for someone from the team to speak to him. I spoke to Mr. Von Hebel and asked for him to obtain that authority, and I understood that effectively because of what has transpired over the last two days, Your Honours wanted written authority in writing -- written authority from Defence counsel that they agreed that someone from the team could see him. As there was no possibility in the time intervening to obtain such authority, nobody has spoken to him at all, and I'm afraid I don't know what the results are or whether he feels fit and able to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it has got nothing to do with what has transpired these last two days. It has to do with the fact that we were not sitting when I received this information. And therefore, this being such a matter of the witness being contacted by an investigator and not for, for example, by someone from the VW section, I told Mr. Von Hebel that it would be better if I have your request in writing and the agreement or disagreement of the Defence in writing before the sitting. And then I was told that there was too short a time for the Prosecution to prepare anything in writing and that the matter would be brought up first thing --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not the Prosecution to prepare. It was the -- the difficulty was getting hold of both Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But anyway, I just want to make it clear that it has got nothing to do with what has transpired. The fact is that I found it a little bit unusual that it would be an investigator to contact this witness rather than someone from the victim's and witnesses section. I mean, this is ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the reason is, Your Honour, that because -- admirable though the victim's and witness's section may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know how it works, to tell you the truth in such circumstances. And I tried to find out from Mr. Von Hebel, and he doesn't know either. He couldn't recall one instance which he was involved on which he could enlighten me. So I said at this point in time, I would rather prefer to have in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I quite understand, Your Honour. I'm merely pointing out the situation. All I'm saying is that perhaps before the witness comes in -- when he comes in, rather, Your Honour could make some inquiries as to whether he feels fit to continue testifying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm open to all suggestions. This is absolutely new to me. I don't know -- and I've tried to find out what has happened in the past. I've been told that most times in the past when something like this happens, it's been the victim's and witness's section that sort of takes control of the situation, keeps the OTP and the Defence informed, and then you inform me. But what to do at this point in time, I am open to any suggestion that you may have. And if there is absolutely no disagreement from the Defence to have an investigator approach --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it could be done -- well, Your Honour, may I say -- and if Mr. Ackerman would be kind enough to let me finish, first of all -- the situation is I think it probably is a bit easier if -- and it may be one of Your Honours' staff now could speak to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is he here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is he here? Oh, I thought he wasn't even here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think so, yes. Because it's a bit -- if he's in court, he's going to say that -- to find out what the state of his health is, whether he does feel able to continue this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean -- I think -- do you have any objection if I direct the registrar to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So Ms. Chuqing Chen, please could you just have -- and do make it clear to him that we are easy and that if he doesn't feel like giving evidence today -- Yes, Madam Fauveau. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. I took it for granted. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I do have an objection to what Ms. Korner just said, because we finished the hearing this morning around noon, and the two Defence teams were present in the Defence room throughout the break and no one contacted us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree. Nobody did contact them, because by the time we got hold of Mr. Von Hebel, it was something like 1.00. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He informed -- he informed me around about 1.00, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. So that's why we took the view that wouldn't have been possible to get all this sorted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, you don't have any objection. So Madam Chuqing Chen, I would just suppose that you just make it clear to him if that he doesn't feel well, he only needs to tell us. I mean, we are not here -- Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to say this for the record and make it a part of a transcript in this case. Situations will arise where it is important for things to be dealt with on a rather almost emergency basis. And as frustrating an advocate as Ms. Korner is at times, I do believe her to be a thoroughly and completely honourable lawyer. So if she represents to Your Honours that she has spoken to me and I have no objection, you may put that in the bank, because it will be the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we wait until Ms. Chuqing Chen comes back, or shall we --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just raise, then, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How far is the witness from the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's very close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very close.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, but there are a couple of matters. I was asked this morning about witnesses not for next week but the week after. Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is one witness, because we're not sitting on the Monday, the 6th of May -- that is, Witness 7.224. Your Honours are going to be provided with his statement today. One of the witnesses from the humanitarian organisation. On Friday, the 10th of May, there will be the legal argument in respect of the journalist. And Your Honour, if there's any time left over, there are I'm sure administrative matters one can deal with. Your Honour, what I wonder if we could have some assistance on -- it's quite clear that Judge Draganovic will not finish in chief today, absolutely not. The -- he is due to return on Monday, the 13th of May. And again, we're not sitting Friday, the 17th. Can I take it that even if we finish in chief with him on the 13th of May, cross-examination will take up the remaining three days? I'm asking for assistance on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, from my standpoint, I -- I seriously doubt it. I haven't heard all of the direct yet. But from what I've heard, my cross-examination would be quite brief. It may be that there will be evidence to come that would require me to cross-examine further, but I can't imagine based upon what I've heard now that it would require a very lengthy cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in the worst case, one day will be sufficient for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, we'll see what arrangements we can make to bring the -- to start the next witness. I mean, the problem -- I suppose in effect we could interpose the legal argument, even if we -- and then have a -- and then start another witness, who can then wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The important thing, Ms. Korner, is that as far as possible, to try and bring and keep witnesses the least possible in The Hague. And that takes, obviously, some planning -- not some. I mean, considerable planning on your -- on your part, more or less what you've been told by the Defence teams now should put you in a position to take stock. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'll make it absolutely clear that none of these witnesses that are coming up are going to give direct -- well, this witness has given direct testimony, as it were, but in hearsay form about General Talic. There's another witness coming thereafter who will give direct evidence of that meeting when General Talic was present. But other than that, this evidence relates to the events that took place in Sanski Most without any direct implication of either accused, only in the sense that there are links which we will be showing through the documents to both accused. If the case is that where there's no direct evidence being given, effectively I may lead a lot of the evidence through. Then that will be of assistance. And it will also speed matters up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With the assistance of the interpreter, I just talked to the witness. Judge Draganovic, and he assured me that he's fit -- very fit to go ahead with this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Anything else before we start?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I mention this only because I don't want to hear someday that I should have mentioned it and didn't. I have yet to hear from -- a response from my latest correspondence with the humanitarian organisation. And there has been more than sufficient time has passed for that to have happened. I have a fear, and I must state that fear for the record, and that is that your ruling allowing these witnesses to testify before I had worked out my arrangements with them has caused them to feel free not to negotiate with me any further. And so I would suggest that you might think about reconsidering that ruling, because I fear that my negotiations with them might be at an end, since there's no longer any impetus for them to do that. I don't know that to be the case, but I'm raising it at this opportunity because there's another -- more than a week now that will go by in this matter, and then the witness will be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to join what Mr. Ackerman has said. We are in contact with the same organisation, and we are in the same situation as Mr. Ackerman; we have absolutely no response from them which would indicate any kind of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just -- [Microphone not activated] I have nothing to say on that matter other than to say that the witness has been arranged and certainly the first one will be coming. There's one other witness who, Your Honour, we've had to fix a date for because of the difficulties. That's Witness 7.52. He's not a protected witness, but I see no benefit in mentioning his name in open court -- who is a businessman. He will be testifying -- has to testify -- I'm just giving advance notice -- on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the -- on Friday, the 21st of June and Monday the 24th, if necessary. He will also be testifying in the Stakic case. He's one of the witnesses that was named on the proposed deposition motion. And the arrangements are that he will go into the Stakic case once he is finished here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you propose to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Call him in chief on Friday, the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are sitting -- because we do have a week off in June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- we have the week off before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's the following week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Could you bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The only other thing is Your Honour may think that maybe it might be an idea not to do a full session even though the witness says he's fit and perhaps think about stopping at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will say -- yesterday, before he comes -- yesterday I was -- I tried to keep two eyes open here, and I was watching him. And there was a moment when he was not exactly what I would have liked to see on my monitor. So if that repeats itself, I will stop the sitting, because there was a moment where perhaps we went a little bit too far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, and welcome back to this Tribunal. Once more, I will have to pass through the usual routine, and you're kindly asked to repeat the solemn declaration to tell us the truth. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, and thank you first. I say that. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down, Judge. Before we start, the registrar came to speak to you to make sure that you -- not only that you are in a condition to give evidence but that you feel that you are in a state to give evidence. And she assures me that you're feeling all right and that you have no problems with continuing with your testimony today. Am I right to assume that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The next thing is if at any time -- if at any time during the course of this afternoon's session you either feel uneasy, tired, awkward, or no longer in a position to continue to give evidence, you -- please do feel free to tell me. I mean, this is a special Tribunal dealing with special events, and we fully understand. And when I say "we fully understand," I can assure you that I'm speaking for the Prosecution and for the Defence. No one wants to put you in a difficult position or to make you feel uneasy in the -- in the witness -- in the witness chair. So Ms. Korner will proceed with the examination-in-chief. And as I said, the moment you would like us to stop, please tell us. Examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry. I'm going to have to ask go on asking you questions about Manjaca camp, as you appreciate. I just want to ask you first of all about the interrogations. First of all, your interrogation. Were you asked to make any kind of a statement?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made a statement. They took us out frequently for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say you made a statement. Was that a document that you signed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a statement, one. I didn't sign anything. This was after eight days, after leaving this solitary cell, isolation cell, the horse shed, they took us all out for interrogation after the beatings, and we waited there in front of the command. And then one by one or in groups they took us in to see various interrogators. Before that, there was physical mistreatment for each one of us I was interrogated. That was the first time at Manjaca -- by an officer, wearing a uniform. He was about 50 years old. He wore a moustache, and he had greying hair. That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can I say -- for the moment what I want to concentrate on the type of statement that you made. Did you -- you say they were questioning you about arms and the like. Did you ever make any admissions to things which were not true?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always spoke the truth. I wasn't afraid. And even then I said that we had lived in a -- under good inter-ethnic relations, that there were absolutely no problems, that all my life I had spent in such an atmosphere, in such an environment. I had been educated in a spirit of commonality. I lived in student hostels together with members of all other ethnicities. I socialised with people of all ethnicities, that I never cared as to who was a Serb or a Muslim or a Croat or whatever religion they may be. I couldn't even distinguish people by their religion, whether they were one or the other. I would say that I was a professional in my work, that I did my job correctly in accordance with the law and the constitution of the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know, because you were told, whether anybody else who was interrogated confessed to doing things they had not done because of the -- the beatings and the violence?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that people signed statements without even knowing what they were signing. I also signed a statement, but maybe a month later. I didn't dare look what was there. They just took me out a month later, and before that they took me out several -- on several other occasions. And I signed that statement, and I don't really know what I signed nor was it read to me nor did I dare read it, because people were beaten whenever they were taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you what may seem to be a silly question, sir. But why did you sign a statement that you hadn't read and didn't know what was in it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why I did, and I keep asking myself why I didn't read that statement. However, at that point in time I felt that this was a decision on which life and death depended, because interrogators had just arrived from Sanski Most, and they asked me -- they asked me whether I had attended a meeting of the police that Avdo Hebib from Sarajevo had attended. In fact, they didn't ask me whether I had attended. They said that I had been present and that I had taken part in the formation of the police, the Muslim police. And there were -- they had some sort of consultations amongst themselves because there were representatives -- there was Rodic, a man called Jugoslav Rodic from Prijedor, and they would go out. I was fearful as to what would happen because I expected to be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you told us yesterday what had happened to you. I'd like to ask you now about what happened to some of the other people in respect of beatings. I will deal with deaths as a separate topic. Did you see other people being beaten?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall try to speak to you about this in some detail, please, because I need to concentrate to be able to do that. Yesterday I didn't say enough, and I thought about it last night. It is hard to put it in a few sentences here. What kind of physical abuse and beatings we experienced is something I had never seen in my whole life, even in the movies up to then, that people could beat other people like that. They were blows meant to kill. Every night -- or rather, every day there were large-scale beatings, and this was particularly in evidence during the first two months. I spoke yesterday about the horse stable, and it was terrible in this horse stable, the kind of beatings we suffered, because in the meantime they brought several groups, because we from Sanski Most were brought on the 23rd. Then they brought some people from Jajce and Mrkonjic Grad. And they would bring to two three men there from each group, and there were such beatings with various objects that people were -- had blood on them. Then they brought a large group to this same horse stable, 60 or 70 people. And then they beat all of them. This was at 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning. I think that these people were brought from Kljuc. These were older men. Unbelievable. They would beat us with cables, with wooden poles, rifle butts, boots. When we were moved to the cow sheds -- but let me tell you about a detail while we were still in the horse shed. One morning before we went -- I went for interrogation, this military policeman called Bula. We were in a group. He took us out. We had to raise our hands up, showing three fingers, these three fingers, like this. And we formed a circle. And then he forced us with our hands raised in this way to drop on the ground with our bodies forward, one by one, and that we had to say outloud, "I am kissing this Serbian soil. I'm a Serb bastard. This is Serbian land." This was for me the greatest humiliation. I would prefer to get a bullet than to have to say that, but I couldn't get a bullet. But I got beatings instead. If anyone were to fall in a wrong -- in the wrong way, or if he would say something wrong, he would be beaten up: Hit in the stomach, in the head with fits. One old man in front of me, he didn't weigh more than 40 kilos. I think he came from somewhere around Mrkonjic Grad. He may have been between 60 and 70 years of age. And I remember this scene. It has stuck in my memory. He fell before me, and he couldn't show these three fingers, but he instead showed these other three fingers. And then this Bula shouted at him, yelled at him, and he jumped on him with his boots, to kick him in the stomach. The man fell down screaming and crying. Then he told him to get up again and to show the three fingers properly. The man couldn't do it. He couldn't get up again. And before my very eyes, he pressed his heel into this area of the kidneys where there was only skin, and he twisted around his heel into this area of his body where his kidney is. And this was terrible. I don't know what happened to that map afterwards. Of course I fell down and did the same thing. I just wanted to describe this for you to show you the way in which they beat us and humiliated us. We had to sing Chetnik songs. When I was transferred to the stables, after the first interrogation, I was all black and blue, all kinds of colours were on me, red, black, and blue from my face, back, chest, legs, stomach. I was all covered in bruises, not just me but everyone else who got into those stables on that day. When I went inside, I saw that those same people were in the stable and their -- they may have numbered some 300, and they also, all of them, had these bruises on their backs and chests. And every day these military policemen would come. And this Bula was the worst, and Zoka, a fair-haired Zoka. There was another one who was dark haired, and other policemen. And also Sinisa. Those three persons were the worst in the physical mistreatment and abuse of people. Every day groups would come in during the day or during the night; sometimes smaller, sometimes larger groups, and no one entered the camp without being beaten up, so badly beaten up that he was black and blue with broken ribs and swellings and haematoma and the like. I could list the names of many people that I knew who entered the camp with such injuries. Within the camp and the stable, every day there was physical mistreatment and beatings several times a day. They would enter two or three times in the course of the day, and they would take all the people in order. The worst -- those who feared worst were those in the middle row on the concrete, because as they walked through the door they would start beating each and every one until they got tired of it. When they tired, they would go away and come back and start all over again. Some people were beaten constantly, every day. People had terrible injuries. When the International Red Cross arrived to see us for the first time, there wasn't a single person that didn't have very serious injuries on his body, bruises on the back, on their faces, and in their chest. People suffered such unbelievable injuries. The worst was night-time. In the evening one wouldn't know who would live to see the day. I couldn't sleep a single night for more than 40 days, maybe 60 days even. I don't know for sure. There was no sleep. Often they would come drunk. Just before nightfall things were quietened down, and then you would start hearing the dogs around the camp. And this was horrific. And then they would come, and they would come to each of the stables. And as there were three stables that were filled at the time in the first camp, first they would go to one, the second, and then the third stable and beat the inmates up. Every night they would take out 10 to 20 men, maybe more even. It's hard to say. We would hear in the lower stable when they beat people in the upper stable. Usually they would call them out from the doorway. They would call them out by name and first name, and people had to go out, leave the stable, and go out in front of the stable. And that is when the beatings began. It was hard to say which was worse, to listen to those screams and those beatings. It's as if you were to take a large carpet and hang it up and beat it with a beater, if you ever did that or heard it, and the blows you make with it make the sounds -- such sounds as we heard when they were beating the people. Then there were moans, cries, crying, screaming, bangs against the door of the stable. Sometimes they would take men outside the camp during that first month. Above the camp, there was a covered area for vehicles, and they would take people there because there were more of them there, and they would beat people, especially the people from Kljuc. They would take them out there. I apologise. Excuse me. When they would finish beating the people in the first stable, then it was the turn for the second stable, the one in the middle. They would open the door. They would call the people to come out from that stable. They had to come out. They would give a list to the person on duty there at the door, and he would read from the list. Then the beatings would start for half an hour, 40 minutes, or -- I don't know for how long. It's difficult to say. And then it was the turn for the lower stables. But not a single night passed without people being called out and being beaten. In the course of the night, people would return to the stables. They would crawl in and take other people in, because after the beatings they were ordered to go back to the stables. Sometimes there were more of them who were beating. We didn't know exactly who participated in them, but there were military policemen, Bula, this fair-haired man called Zoka, Spaga, and others whose names I will mention. Soldiers would come wearing uniforms. I mentioned someone who was fully equipped. He had a helmet on which there were some kinds of ornaments. I'm not a soldier, so I don't know what it is exactly, but some sort of camouflage which conceals the helmet, and he was a strong Serbian soldier. Many of them came on several occasions to beat people. I don't know where they came from, whether it was from the barracks down below or whether they were in the barracks there, whether they were the guards. When they started standing guard duty -- when the policemen started going on guard duty, policemen who would come from the public security stations of the various municipalities, I can say that the people from Kljuc are the ones who were beaten, together with the military policemen. And I can say that I didn't notice that these policemen who came from Sanski Most -- I didn't notice that they participated in the beatings of people in this way, when they were on guard. I didn't hear this from anyone, from any of the inmates. As I said, these beatings lasted for a long time. Sometimes they would get tired. They would fall into a sort of box, and then they would take it in turns to beat people. Some people were lucky and wouldn't be beaten on that occasion, but he would be beaten on another occasion. Every week -- I think it was a Sunday -- they would come en masse and they would make all of us leave the stables, and we would have to line up ten by ten and we would have to crouch down, and they would then enter the stables to inspect them. This took place every week. They inspected them, just to see that we hadn't brought anything in. They scattered everything they could find there. I don't know what they were looking for exactly. They were searching for something. Then the people would be called out in front of the door to each stable, the entrance to each stable, and they would call each person out, ask each person to go in. Everyone had to enter the stable very quickly; otherwise, he would be beaten. And as each person entered the stable, they would search these people. We all had to stand like this. And then they would beat us while we were entering the stable. And then they would let the people enter. Everyone was treated in this way. This took place every week, and we all received beatings. Not a single person was spared these beatings. Sometimes the beatings lasted for a long time and were very severe, and sometimes they were not so severe. And then when it would rain, they would often make us leave the stables, and we would have to stand there in the rain getting wet. Sometimes we would stand there in the rain for two or three hours or more. And when we were completely drenched, they would drive us back into the stables. And naturally, in the stables there was earth and concrete and water, and we would have to lie down in that kind of a state. I don't know what -- what we could call this -- or rather, I do, because everyone had to wait for these clothes to dry. But how could this happen? That would take days. If you would allow me just to describe something else. While I was in those stables and when they would bring groups of those poor people from fields, from their houses and -- I don't know where they would bring them from, from buses. They were taken off buses too and brought there. In the lower stable in which I was kept, stable number 1, after a few days they brought a group -- a big group from Kljuc there. And that was terrible. The people would enter the stables. It was dark. They put the light on somehow. They seldom do that. They seldom did that. But on that occasion, they did put the light on. They brought those people in a -- in a truck from Gornja Sanica. And they were between 16 or 17 years of age up until about 70 or 80. There were old people there, senile people. Then the beatings would start outside, inside. They were thrown in through the door, and they would beat them as they were entering them. It was necessary to pass the metal fence. You had to bend over, and then you would be hit on the back with a -- with a plank. I don't know with what. And they shoved the people into those boxes. Not everyone was able to fit in. They shoved a group into the box in which we were kept. I was facing the wall towards the bottom of the stables. And then these people on the other side from the ditch, they made them lie down there and placed their heads down on the floor. And you can imagine what it looked like. That area only had one square metre, and there was stone on the ground and pebbles, very sharp pebbles. That was half the area. And the other half of the area was concrete, perhaps 10 centimetres more elevated than the other half. And people had to lie down there, and I saw that with my own eyes. We had to look down, but we weren't allowed to look at what was happening, but I looked at it secretly. And they would shove people's faces into those -- into that pebble ground. It's impossible to imagine that. It's impossible to imagine people doing such things. Naturally I met all those people. I became acquainted with them. And their injuries were terrible. They'd all been through the same things. We had all been through the same things. Every day the same sort of abuse would take place. We would be called out, taken away for interrogation. We would be beaten. We would be put in the isolation cells and beaten there. Whoever was taken to an isolation cell -- all the isolation cells were always full of people. Everyone had to stay in an isolation cell. Beatings took place in these isolation cells every evening. The isolation cell is about 50 metres away from me. We could hear every blow, every scream. And all of us in the stables lived through this. It was terrible. It's impossible to say whether it was worse to listen to this or to be beaten. The injuries some people sustained were terrible, and they went out with these injuries. They left the camp, those who survived, with these injuries. Some were killed. Some were taken away; we don't know where. But all I can say is that this was a death camp. It was a death camp. Their goal was to kill all of us, to make sure that we no longer existed. That's what they told us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that? Who told you that their goal was that you should no longer exist?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military policemen told us this, the military policemen who came in on a daily basis. They had prepared this propaganda, and they would what they would tell us. They told us that we weren't a people. They said that we were going to be like the Palestinians that -- our fate would be worse than theirs. They said, "You want a state? Here is a state for you." They told us, "Here and your Alija Izetbegovic," et cetera, et cetera. Every day they had prepared speeches. And when they came to give us these speeches -- to make these speeches, they beat us. As I say, this lasted for 60, 70 days. It's difficult to say how long exactly. But I could mention some periods up until the time when Omer Filipovic and others were killed, up until when the International Red Cross came to carry out a sort of registration and up until the appearance of the journalists, because when the International Red Cross and the journalists arrived, things changed. But I forgot how to sleep. I wasn't able to sleep. When night fell, death appeared too. I didn't think I was going to survive. It's possible to talk about these things for a long time. I could expand on this, but I think that other people -- other inmates will speak about this too. Since you're going to ask me about killings, I'll answer your questions about this subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before we get on to that, can I just ask you about a couple of the things you've mentioned. First, you've mentioned this man Bula. Did you discover what his name -- his real name was?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his name was Zeljko Bulatovic. But again, I'm not a hundred per cent sure because they would hide their real names. They had nickname z of some kind. They had several nicknames. But I figured out that that was his name. But I'm not absolutely certain of this, because he is -- one of his nicknames was Fadil. Another one was Bula. Then he had a third nickname it was Tito. I can describe him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that. Were you interviewed by the German authorities in respect of this man?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him? Was he ever prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he wasn't, not in Republika Srpska -- that is to say in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know of any proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned this man you called Spaga. Who was Spaga? What level of authority did he have in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would you allow me to use some of my notes in order to be certain of the names, to avoid making any errors? If I may. If not, I'll just say what I can remember, because I made notes, and I do have these notes in my pocket.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if he may be allowed to use his notes to refresh his memory if he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he's going to use notes, I think a copy should be made for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge, do you have any objection at all if you are allowed to make reference to your notes to make a copy of those notes available to the Defence and to the Prosecution, obviously, and also to the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's just a piece of paper, an ordinary piece of paper. I didn't prepare anything in particular. I made a list of names -- of the names I know of in order to avoid any error. But if necessary, I can copy it. It's no problem. It's just an ordinary piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is just to help me to be precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. No. I'll explain to you the procedure of this Court. Usually when a witness asks to be allowed to consult notes, personal notes, usually the practice is that permission is granted on condition that those notes are also made accessible to whoever wants to check. So perhaps Madam Registrar, we could -- Madam Registrar -- you could make reference to the notes and then we will make a copy of them and have them -- have them handed over to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man you called Spaga, again do you know what he -- did you ever discover what his real name was and what position he held in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found out what his name was. I found out what his real name was. He's from Banja Luka. I know that he lives in Banja Luka now too and that he was a private businessman in the catering business. And it's quite possible that this is still what he does now in Banja Luka. His name is Predrag Kovacevic aka Spaga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he -- did he hold any position of authority in the camp that you could see higher than an ordinary guard?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was a command of the guards in the camp, and they would call him "warden" and whatnot. But he was the person who entered the camp every day and at all times of the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person in charge of the camp was a man named Colonel Popovic. Did you see him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Bozidar Popovic was a lieutenant colonel in the JNA, and I knew that he was the commander of the camp. I can describe him. He entered the camp occasionally. But most of the time he was in the command and in the surroundings of the camp. We would see him when he arrived, when he left. He had a -- a driver. He was driven around in a Lada car which had been taken from a Bosnian from Kljuc who had been killed, someone called Spreco. So he drove around in that car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he came into the camp, was that into the precincts where the prisoners were -- the areas where the prisoners were?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He came in on several occasions. He came in very often. If some delegation came to visit, he was always with that delegation. He went into all the stables. He would make the rounds of the entire camp. He went into the horse shed too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he ever present when a beating was taking place? If you can't remember one way or the other, then say so.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I only saw him when a group from Prijedor was brought in, from Omarska. I saw him on that occasion, when they took the people out there and when they killed them, he was there on the grounds. I saw him from -- in that area, but I can't remember seeing him in that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to that incident about the killing. But when he was there, were there prisoners open to view by anybody who had injuries, visible injuries?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was there every day. He saw us inmates every day. I have a sketch of this camp here. People were taken away for interrogation on a daily basis. They would stand by the wall. And when they took people for interrogations, they would first of all be beaten. He must have seen that. It's just not possible for him not to have seen that. He heard people groaning. Every day Bula and Zoka, Oseka, Sinisa, and others someone called Popovic Alexander, Cukic [phoen]. When they went to the isolation cell to beat the people who were confined there, he knew they were going to beat them there because they would beat people before they were interrogated, before they were questioned. They kept people for days in those isolation cells and beat them every day several times. Yesterday I spoke about the fact that I experienced the same thing. But I know people who -- who were treated even worse than I was, people who were killed too. Omer Filipovic -- the late Omer Filipovic on one occasion when he was taken to the isolation cell, he stayed there had for 18 days. I heard them beating Omer Filipovic every day. He was so tough he didn't cry, he didn't scream, he didn't groan. He put up with it stoically until -- until he died. And I'm just talking about this with regard to whether Popovic knew about this, to show whether he knew about this, because he knew everything. He saw us every day. He saw us through the -- through the fence, because his command, his window faced our stables, and he could see us when we passed by with our heads bowed down and our arms behind our backs. Naturally he could see us. Every day we were taken away to do forced labour. Thousands of men were taken away to do forced labour every day. From morning until night this is hard labour. You haven't asked me any questions about food yet, what the food is like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we'll talk about food in 15 minutes' time. Judge, we'll give you a rest for 15 minutes, and we'll resume immediately after that. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness had two pages of notes, and we've been given a copy of only one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you have two pages?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No. It is only one page note.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean, I'm sitting right here. He had two pages out when he asked if he could refer to his notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But if he's going to refer to one page only, I mean, that's what you'll get.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm just making sure that we have got --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you have two pages or one page? Just one page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last sentence of this first page referring to Manjaca does not end, so I assume that there's a second page that is relative to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a second page, Judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I asked to look at this page only to remind myself of the names. I didn't take out the second page because it doesn't matter. I won't look at it. I don't need it. And since we are talking about the camp, so as not to leave out any names or mention them incorrectly, I have them noted down here when I concentrated and took note of them, should I need them. But there's no problem for me to have the second page copied, but I won't be using it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you dealt with Colonel Popovic. Did any other officers that you saw -- senior officers come to Manjaca while you were there? And I mean military. I'm going to come on to political figures later.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed especially at first that military delegations did come, or rather, officers, army officers came. And they even entered the stable. They looked around and turned back, as did the camp commander. And it was -- it is hard to say how many times, but they did come. Civilian persons came too, civilian leaders from Banja Luka whom I recognised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to talk about the civilian leaders later, as I said I want to deal with them as a group. Did you know by sight any of the senior officers or from seeing them on television, any of the senior officers in the 1st Krajina Corps, or the 5th, as it was earlier on?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you that from the 1st -- or rather, 5th Krajina Corps, that I didn't know the officers except if I saw them on television. But I knew General Talic also by sight from television, but I didn't know other people by name. I didn't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever see General Talic at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that General Talic came to visit the camp once, but I do allow for the possibility that I may be wrong because when officers came, most frequently when a delegation came, be it a military one or any other kind, the order was for the doors of the stables to be closed and no one was allowed out, so everyone had to be inside, except when they entered the stables to see them. It seems to me that General Talic was there once, and he knows best whether he was or not. I think this was sometime around the end of June, the beginning of July or in July. I think so. That was when dugouts were made with machine-guns at the corners of the camp on all sides, and there were machine-guns positioned there and an observation post had been erected above the camp, and a soldier was stationed there to observe things. And it seems to me that I saw him on that observation post, but I do allow for the possibility that I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you able -- if you were in the stables and the doors were shut, how were you able to see that someone was on the observation post?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assigned to working in the canteen, helping in preparing the food, so I was outside the stable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I haven't quite finished on the beatings yet. But you referred to a plan of Manjaca. Can you have a look at what was attached to your statement as attachment number 7?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is in fact the same as P467.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us whether that's the plan you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the sketch, the detailed sketch of the camp within the wire fence. It's a well-made sketch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you, please, if you could --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not you, Mr. Draganovic. And could you just indicate which barn you were held in.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first barn. That was the lower one within the first camp, and I was inside this one in the -- on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know whether Your Honours want him to mark that and make it an exhibit or whether it's sufficient simply if he's indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, Ms. Korner. Judge, could I kindly ask you to draw an arrow marking the shed or stable that according to you were kept in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And put your initials, please, next to that arrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that then be made Prosecutor's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Exhibit 760, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just one other aspect on the beatings generally which you've described in such detail. You said that people were called out. Was there any, as it were, targeting of people who you described as leaders in the community who were being called out or singled out for these beatings, or did it apply to everybody?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I mentioned these call-outs, especially at night, they would call out mostly people who were leaders of parties or who held certain positions. And between 10 and 20 men would leave one of these sheds almost every night until Bender and Filipovic's death. Also, within the stable when the military policemen came -- mostly it was Bula, Zoka, and Sinisa -- they always or most frequently selected those people and would beat them first and then the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the deaths. There were, I think, a number of incidents. So can we divide them. First of all, how many people -- I don't mean exact numbers, but what incidents of these beatings resulted in death of the prisoner?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- considering all those killed -- that were killed at Manjaca, and those who were choked during transportation, and those who were taken away alive from Manjaca in trucks and whose traces are lost and whom I consider to have been killed, so I can roughly add all those up and it would amount to between 60 and 80 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we deal first of all with people who died as a result of these beatings. And let's start with Omer Filipovic, who you've mentioned. Were you present when he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present several times when he was beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the specific incident that led to his death?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say first of all what preceded this event in the camp. The International Red Cross came on a visit, and representatives of the International Red Cross entered the sheds so that the military policemen were outside the sheds. And the representatives of the International Red Cross would speak to people one on one, examine their injuries, the injuries on their bodies. Even though there was fear, people would show their injuries and their suffering. On that day -- or rather, the previous day Omer Filipovic was brought back from the isolation cell where he had spent, I think, 18 days, something like that. That was his second solitary confinement. And throughout the period he spent in solitary confinement, he was beaten up there. And I heard the beating, and I saw them leave -- the policemen, the military policemen -- when they went to beat him. On that day when the International Red Cross was due to come, a part of the stall that I was in the first stable -- there were 30 of us, and we were forced out of that part of the stable and forced to go to the other side closer to the door, so that this area that was now empty, that is where they put Omer Filipovic and he had to face the wall. He was not allowed to look towards the rest of us, and that is how he stood when the International Red Cross arrived. And then a representative of the International Red Cross spoke to Omer Filipovic. After that -- I'm afraid I can't remember exactly whether it was after two, three, or five days, but anyway the International Red Cross was due to come again. They had announced they would come on Wednesday to bring registration cards with them because we were supposed to be given numbers. And that night just before they arrived Omer was again in isolation, mistreated and beaten there, and that day, the day that he was killed -- that they beat him during the day. And he was covered in blood and beaten up with injuries. They beat him in the isolation cell. And two inmates led him, supporting him on each side. They literally carried him along. He couldn't walk. They dragged him along. He was so badly hurt. And I stood in the immediate vicinity because they passed by me. I was working in the kitchen at the time. That evening when the roll call was done, I was in this stable in the stall, in the box when they called out, among others, Omer Filipovic, telling him to come out straight away. My first thought was that he was unable to go out because he had already been beaten up. However, Omer answered loudly, "Yes, I'm coming out," and he ran from the end of the stable over people's feet, and he came out of the stable. Other people were called out too that night, including myself. However, I didn't go out, nor did some others go out. But those who went out that night, Bender Esad -- I think it was Esad -- a relative of mine, Kemal Draganovic went out; Senad Supuk from Sanski Most went out -- Bajro Supuk. I can't remember all the names. And a terrible thing started outside. They beat them behind the stable closer to the horse shed outside. And the blows were echoing, and they used all kinds of objects -- wooden objects. Every blow was followed by a scream. And this went on for a long time, maybe for two hours. I heard them running -- the policemen running. I heard their shoes. They were carrying buckets of water, pouring water on the men. I heard their steps several times, the steps of the military policemen. And around midnight one of them came to the door of the stable and called out a detainee, Dr. Mehmed Derviskadic who was a friend of mine and he was lying right next to me. We were one next to another -- our bodies were one next to another. Of course we were all in fear, and he was the one that night who kept me from going out. He lay on top of me and said, "If you go out, they'll kill you." And he went out. He didn't come back for a long time. And he came back around 2.00 -- I don't know exactly -- 2.00 a.m. at night, but they -- he was called every night when groups came. And I was always waiting for him to come back. When he came back, he was in shock. He was frightened. He was out of his mind. He whispered in my ear so that others wouldn't hear, "Omer and Bender and Senad Supuk have been killed, and someone else too." That night I learnt from him that they had been killed. However, Senad fell into a garbage pit, and he lost consciousness. He fainted down there. The pit was about 2 or 3 metres deep, and there were metal tins and garbage there, and they probably couldn't pull him out then, and Senad, when he came to, when he regained consciousness in the morning, he crawled back into the stable. We saw then the injuries. Bajro Supuk also and all the others who went out, they fared worse that night. In the morning they wouldn't let us go out. The doors had to be kept closed. The doctor asked me then what he should do. He said that he had to sign a death certificate confirming that they had died of natural causes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just stop you. Was that the doctor you mentioned, Derviskadic, or another doctor?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Derviskadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. Go on.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning he was called out again to go outside. I saw the military investigations commission arrive from Banja Luka, as in the morning I was where the kitchen was, I saw them. And they went to the horse shed. I think to the left-hand side of the isolation cell. And they carried out an investigation over there. I saw that they had a camera and that they took photographs. Then a military vehicle arrived, and they carried out the bodies and carried them away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, either at that period or at any stage later, has anyone ever been prosecuted for the deaths of Filipovic and Bender?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that no one was, nor were any proceedings instituted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about just one other incident as an example of what you saw before we come to the suffocation incident. Was there an occasion when a group from the Kljuc area, specifically from the village of Krasulje were brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krasulje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Was somebody killed or did somebody die as a result of what happened that evening?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the break, I spoke about the group that was brought in, and that's the group from Krasulje, Kljuc municipality. In that group was a young man who was between 21 and 23 years old. He was really a handsome young man, like a film star, wearing a white shirt and black trousers and rubber boots. He was right next to me, very close to me. I saw that he had already been beaten, that he had come with some injuries. When the policemen left, I took him in so that he could lie in my place. On the 12th day, he succumbed. He was beaten. I think he had an injury of his chest. His name was Husein Delalovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, just one more incident. Was there also a man in the camp with you named Emir Mulalic who was a policeman from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Emir Mulalic is a policeman who was thrown out of the public security station on that day, the 17th of April, that I spoke about the other day. He was also arrested and brought to Manjaca. He was also killed by beating, and this happened during interrogations in the command. He was beaten by military policemen. Twice in the same day, while the interrogation went on, he was interrogated by a police inspector from Sanski Most, Brane Sobot -- Brane Sobot and another police inspector from Sanski Most. He was beaten up while he was being questioned by him. Then they took him out, and then in the hallway they beat him again, and that is where he was killed. They beat him -- that is, Spaga, Bula, Sinisa, I think the three of them -- but a witness who was present when he was being beaten can tell you best, because Spaga beat him after he had passed away already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can I ask you about the deaths as a result of the suffocation on the way to Manjaca. Did you personally witness any of that incident, any part of it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the camp, and they were being transported on the 7th of July. And a lot of people from Sanski Most were taken to Manjaca in trucks. They were all civilians who had been imprisoned from the 27th of May in the sports hall in Sanski Most, in Betonirka, the Betonirka garage. Some of them were in the prison of the public security station. Some were in -- in the Krings hall. The people who were -- who were suffocated, they had already been treated in Sanski Most. And when I say "treated," I mean physically abused. These people mostly came from Betonirka, and they were all in one lorry. At the time I was in the stables that evening. That was on the 6th, in the evening. The military police -- I don't know whether it was the fair-haired man called Zoka -- and I'll tell you why I distinguish between the fair-haired Zoka and the dark-haired Zoka. There were three Zokas, but I don't know what their surnames really were, so this is how I distinguished them, because they behaved toward people different too. Someone called doctors to come out. Dr. Meho Derviskadic and Dr. Eniz Sabanovic were asked to come out immediately. They were both inmates from Sanski Most. They went out. And we had previously heard through the walls -- that is to say, we saw the shadows cast by the light when the lorries were coming. There were new inmates coming, but we didn't know who was coming. But we knew that several lorries were arriving. They stopped over at the command for a long time. I can't remember what time it was at night when Derviskadic approached me. He seemed quite lost, and he told me once again, "It was terrible. It was terrible. Our people have been killed, suffocated, a lorry full of them. I counted 17 dead bodies." He told me the names. I immediately found out the names of these people. He told me that they were loaded onto the lorry again, that this camp commander Popovic ordered that they should be returned there, and even people who were in a very serious condition from other lorries, he also ordered them to return to the lorries, and he said that three -- two or three men who remained alive were sent back to help those who had been injured. And among them was a doctor. He hadn't yet graduated, the son of Faik Biscevic. The other people entered the camp in the morning, and that lorry returned. We knew that there were between 24 and 28 people there. They never appeared again, not even those who remained alive and who were left. In 1995 and afterwards, I tried to find the location of that cemetery, since as an investigating judge I had certain information, according to which that cemetery was located in Krkojevac. On several occasions, I tried to find it by digging, but without any success. It wasn't until 2000, the year 2000 that I managed to find a man who showed me that location. We organised an exhumation. We found 20 bodies. We didn't find all the bodies. That grave was concealed, and it was about 6 kilometres from Sanski Most in the Sanski River canyon, on the left bank of the river, between the local road which goes to Kljevci and the coast. And the ground had been leveled there so it was impossible to know that that's where the location was. So the other people who were still alive in the lorry, who had been sent back from Manjaca and the doctor who returned, these people were never found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was one of the people who was killed in that transport the president of the misdemeanour court, Nedzad Muhic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nedzad Muhic was the president of the misdemeanour court and when this exhumation was carried out, I recognised his body. He had a brother, Rano, and they were both suffocated -- they were both -- they both suffocated in that transport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, unless there are any other particular incidents that you would like the Court to know about, I would like to move on to deal with other aspects of the camp.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you're going to ask me some questions, I would prefer to respond to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about medical treatment. You mentioned two doctors. What medical supplies were available to these doctors -- no. I'll start again. Were the doctors allowed to administer treatment to people who had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to answer that question. In order for some of the inmates to get to see a doctor, to be examined, it was necessary to register in the afternoon to be put down on a list in the afternoon, and the person who was on guard in the stables would hand over that list to the police at the gate. The police then called out those people and would check -- would check them. They would even beat them. And it was only if the police authorised this that it was possible for the people to go and see a doctor in the morning outside the grounds of the camp. So this was at the command. But that only started functioning a little later. In the beginning, maybe for a month, two months -- I don't know exactly -- although there were doctors in the camp, they were treated in the same way as all the other inmates, and they were with us in the stables -- in the barns. And no medical care had been organised at that time, but they would approach people of their own accord. They would give them advice, tell them what to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing to -- nothing had been organised to help people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to hear evidence from others about the medical aspect. Can I then deal with food, that you mentioned before the break. What was the food like? How often did you get fed, and was it adequate?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I would like to add a few things about the medical treatment in order to be more precise. So I want to be quite clear. A little later -- I can't say exactly when -- I think that in this outpatient clinic and at the command outside the grounds of the camp they had some sort of medicine, tablets mainly. I don't know where these tablets had been obtained from, whether from the command of the -- of the camp or from Merhamet, the charity organisation, or from somewhere else. But at the time it was possible for people to obtain some pills. But this occurred very seldom. Not everyone could get them. A few people were able to get them sometimes. Later when the International Red Cross arrived, the situation improved. But as far as food is concerned, it should be sufficient to say that every inmate from the 1st of June, when the camp was established -- it was about the 1st of June, 1992 -- so from that date up until the arrival of the International Red Cross, every single inmate lost between 20 and 25 kilogrammes. If I say that two meals were provided, well, these meals were just completely insubstantial. As I worked in the kitchen where I prepared the food, I know how much bread was provided for each meal. One slice of -- one loaf of bread, under a kilo. They would cut this loaf up for between 25 to 40 people. So one of those minute slices -- it was barely a slice. It was transparent. It was between half a centimetre and a centimetre thick and about 5 by 6 centimetres. So that was a very small amount of bread, and that's the amount you would get twice a day. I have forgotten certain things, but there are certain things that I can remember. In the beginning, they would get this little piece of bread and half a cup of tea. The tea was made in -- in a military mobile kitchen. That's where they would stoke up a fire. That's where they would boil water. And this was made out of -- this was made out of rose hip, and it would be cooked for over a month. The same rose hip -- they would make tea out of the same rose hip. It was just warm water. There was no sugar at all, until the International Red Cross arrived. And there was another meal in the course of the day. So this was just a tiny slice of bread. It was barely a crumb. And there was some kind of broth which was prepared in a primitive way out of what we had. Initially the aid provided by the Merhamet was very important to us. They would bring vegetables, cabbage, potatoes, occasionally meat. But meat was provided very seldom. On the whole, we received some kind of soya. We had beans. When we got beans, that would be for a holiday of some kind. But there was never a sufficient amount of anything. The portions were minute. We didn't get a third meal. People had to do hard labour. About a thousand people a day would leave the stables. And when they would call from the command, when Spaga, some of the military policemen called from the command and asked for a 1.000 people to come out -- 1.000 people had to come out in five minutes time from all of the stables. On one occasion, five people were missing. Twenty of them entered the stables. They had prepared -- prepared themselves, and they entered with clubs, metal rods, and they beat up the entire camp. All of the inmates were beaten. There were many people who were injured, and they beat people all over their bodies. They had injuries to their heads, arms, broken arms, broken ribs, injuries to the ribs. There was a lot of bleeding. I saw a lot of people who were covered in blood there. And the only reason for this was that five people hadn't come out. People went to work in the fields. I myself went to dig for potatoes there. From 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning, that's when we would go into the fields, up until the afternoon, in the very hot sun. We had been -- our hair had been cut very short. We had been beaten. Many people were ill. Others went to the woods to collect heavy timber. Military policemen and soldiers came from Banja Luka. Orders would be issued every day for the soldiers. They were told to load lorries with timber, to fell trees. They would fell the trees, and the inmates would carry the timber in the forest. There were heavy logs that had to be carried. They were beaten in the woods while they were carrying the timber. They would fall off the lorries while the timber was being transported. And then people also -- people were also involved in building a church very near the camp. This lasted for two or three months. I don't know for how long exactly. They worked all day long, up until the evening, and they had very little food. They did other sorts of work, because in that area, on those grounds there were stables with cattle. And at that time the 1st Corps -- what we called the 1st Corps at the time, they brought all the property that we had in the Bosnian villages to that -- to those grounds, all our cattle. Over 5.000 heads of cattle were brought there, and an enormous number of sheep and of goats. The livestock died outside. Every day lorries would arrive from Banja Luka, from slaughterhouses. We had to load this livestock into lorries. We had to feed this livestock too. And we did other kinds of jobs too. And now that we're talking about food, I said that there wasn't enough sugar. I would like to say that during certain periods, there was no salt either because we wouldn't be given salt. Dr. Derviskadic explained to me that this was deliberate, because if you don't have enough salt, people become aggressive. The metabolism becomes disturbed. And sometimes we would go without salt for 15 days. Please allow me to say something else. When this food would be prepared, we would go out, we would be in lines. We'd leave each stable. We would bow our heads, and our arms would be behind our backs. The military police was always present there. And if anyone raised his head, he would be beaten immediately in front of all of us. These beatings were terrible. We would be kicked in the chest with -- in the head. We'd be kicked in the most sensitive parts of the body. Very often they would make one inmate beat another one. And if he didn't beat the other inmate sufficiently badly, he would be beaten by the police. People would fall down. They were helpless. When food was distributed, when people ate, they ate from dirty plates because there was no water. And the dishes weren't washed. The humiliation was terrible. I saw people eating grass. They would take the grass and eat it. There was no grass anywhere in the camp because every blade of grass was eaten. Between the stables, in a small area, septic pits had been dug, and we would use them to relieve ourselves. These pits were about 3 metres deep, about 2 to 5 metres long, and this is where we would relieve ourselves. We would use a plank. The stables were on a -- on a slight slope, so the upper stable is a little more elevated, about -- it's about 1 metre higher or 2 than the lower stable. And between the stables, there were these pits, these septic pits. When one of them was full, we would dig another one, and then a third one. We dug all these pits. So that between the stables, in those areas, there was these pits and excrement, and this is where grass would grow, and this is grass that we would eat. This camp number one and then camp number two, they were separated by a fence and minefields. This was a very small area, a rectangular area, a square area perhaps, about 100 metres long on one side, 50 or 100 metres long on the other side, so 100 by 100 metres at the most. They were surrounded by minefields and a fence, and artillery guns were pointed because there were cannons and anti-aircraft artillery down below. There were machine-guns in dugouts in the camp itself by the fence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to stop you there, but we're getting rather away from the subject and I wanted to deal with it in the round of the food. I just want to go back for one minute to something you said a little time ago now when the five men refused to come out or didn't come out of the barns in the morning. You said 20 men, they came in with these iron bars. Who were they? I mean, who were these people?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were military policemen and assistants of theirs. They all entered, and they were all involved in the beatings, and we were all beaten, all of us in one of the stables. Only because five people did not go out. There were disabled people, people who after those beatings remained seriously disabled. And I would just like to add before I forget this, that after this time in the camp, a large number of people died in Bosnia or abroad, and these were people who aged between 30 and 40 years -- between 30 and 50 years. I think that at least 200 or 300 people died from that group, and I don't know if you're going to ask me how many people were detained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I -- now you raise it, I will. If you have the figures -- although we have other evidence about it -- how many people were detained there? If you could just give us the number.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew what the approximate number was, as I was in the kitchen and I distributed the bread in camp number 1. I know how many people there were in camp number 2 too. But I know the exact number of people who passed through that camp from the 1st of June up until the 18th of December. That's about 5.434 people.
