utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, we've come off the subject slightly. But as you've raised this, of those people that you were in the camp with, how many of them had been arrested or caught actually fighting, actually involved in fighting against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were mostly civilians who were arrested in their homes, who were brought from villages, from towns. These were not people who were fighting. These were civilians, all of them. I saw them bring in several soldiers too. I saw two members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were brought in as military prisoners. They were peasants. I spoke to them later. And they were later exchanged. There was another soldier, maybe an officer of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who was caught at Jajce or Zenica. And I also knew two or three officers of the Croatian army who were captured somewhere near Bugojno. A member of HOS was brought in. I heard of that. And I heard that he was killed in the -- in solitary confinement. The rest were civilians. They were all civilians. So there were no men there who were resisting the Serbian army or anything else. Later on when Jajce fell, when the Serbs gained control of it, another group of soldiers were brought there who were Serbs by ethnicity. I didn't really know who they were, whether they were deserters from the Army of Republika Srpska or something else. I know that they stayed behind when we were released. So they stayed in the Serbian army. And there were two other Serb soldiers -- one or two -- who were also deserters from the Serb army and who were with us in the stable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you just explain to the Trial Chamber, who may not have heard that expression before, what HOS is, H-O-S.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HOS stands for the Croatian defence forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were units of the territorial defence of Croats who were actually at first defending their villages. However, later on they either joined the Croatian Defence Council, HVO, or the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can I just go back for a brief moment to the question of nutrition in general. You've said -- you've explained about there was no water to wash the plates, and so you had to eat food from dirty plates. Were you given facilities to wash, to have showers of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a chance to have a bath very rarely. I can't be very specific whether it was once a month or once in two months. They would bring in a water tank from Banja Luka by the military units, and there in the camp they would set up showers outside. And then we would have three minutes to pass under those showers with cold water. But as I was saying, this was very rare, but it did exist. At first there was water, the first few days. There was certain installations in the camp because this used to be an agricultural estate. However, this was switched off, and there was no more water. We then had to carry water from the lake. We were given buckets by the International Red Cross, and we would go out, led by the military policemen, in a line as far as the artificial lake. It was dirty, polluted water with tadpoles inside. It was yellow in colour. And then 100 or 200 of us would come, and while filling up those buckets we would muddy the water even further. The second group that would come after us would have to use that muddied water. We would drink that water and we would cook the food with that water and we used it for hygiene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about drinking water? Where did that come from? Did you get any?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, as I was saying -- so when I moved from the isolation cell to shed number 1, we were given water in an army cup or -- and we would share it out amongst ourselves. But that was not sufficient. In a jerrycan which we would pour into a cup later on. However, this was water from the regular supply network that existed at the time. Later on, this network was totally switched off. And as far as I can recollect, maybe the water tank came. I think it did. A military tank -- truck with water. Later we were given these jerrycans or buckets, and we carried the water from the lake, and this was the water that we also drank. After that -- but this was near the end, maybe in August or September -- there were some taps made, water taps. I think that every shed had two or three of these water taps. But I can't remember now. I think it was the International Red Cross that provided these. They brought some large containers with water. And then we were able to pour that water from those taps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when winter came on? Because you were there till December. Were you provided with extra bedding or clothing or anything of that nature by the camp authorities?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the camp authorities, in those stables there was earth and concrete on the floor, maybe a bit of hay or some bushes that we cut outside and collected and laid out on the floor. We did receive some blankets from Merhamet but very few, so that there would be one blanket to five or six men. And we would lay it out on the floor and lie on it. Afterwards, when the International Red Cross came, then we got blankets, sufficient quantities, if one could call it that, two or three blankets. So we could put one below us and cover ourselves with another, so that everyone had one or two blankets. From the International Red Cross --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask about, then, the aid that Merhamet was delivering. Did you receive all of the -- well, what happened when aid was delivered? Perhaps you can tell us that.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Merhamet occasionally, using a blue Deutz 5-tonne lorry would bring some food and clothing that they had collected. This was aid of Muslim citizens in Banja Luka organised by members of the Merhamet. Via Merhamet, we occasionally received parcels from family members. So these parcels started arriving perhaps after a month. I don't know exactly when. But I remember the first Merhamet lorry arriving. I recognised it outside. I recognised the neighbour of mine from Sanski Most, Brkljac. A tall man. He used to be a football player. And I saw them unloading the parcels in front of the entrance on the road. It's hard to say how much there was, but like this area here shall we say, a circle, the circular area in front of me. Then the Merhamet truck drove off, and the military policeman examined those parcels and that's what they did each time. Each parcel would be examined, and they would take what they wanted. In most cases cigarettes, some sweets, if there were any, or a piece of clothing. After that, they would make a list, and that list would be read out to people in the stables telling them that they had parcels. And then those detainees would go out to pick up their parcels. I received a parcel once from my aunts in Banja Luka, and half of it had been taken and half left. How often these parcels arrived, it is hard to say, but maybe weekly or once in a fortnight, on Wednesdays -- I don't know which day. But it was significant. For hygiene, I know that we once received those small soaps -- red soaps. They were all the same. We couldn't all get one. There wasn't enough to go around. As far as I remember, this was sent by Caritas. That was all, until the UNHCR brought us some French soaps. We were filthy, and we had insects and lice. However, later on we did our best to clean ourselves up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Finally on the topic of the conditions and the food. When you entered Manjaca, how much did you weigh?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested in Sanski Most weighing about 90 kilogrammes, and I think I lost between 20 and 30 kilogrammes, from the time of my arrest after two months -- when I was at Manjaca. Later on, when I left I had about 70 or 75 kilos. But the International Red Cross or the UNHCR started bringing in aid. Then the food improved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I don't know what the situation is, whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The situation was like this, Ms. Korner. I was obviously following the direct examination and watching the witness at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a few more -- what I'm really asking is -- I have a few more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he can take a little -- a few more questions, and then I think we better stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what I was about to say was if Your Honour and the interpreters can manage, I can complete the Manjaca thing before 6.00, because I'm going to now deal with simply with the visitors and then ask him to look at the video. I'm in Your Honours' hands. If Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. How long would you expect that to last?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would imagine between -- I should think another half hour or so. But Your Honour, I'm in Your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go ahead for the time being, and then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, Judge, sometime ago some of the military officers who came -- or the military who came to the camp. Were there also visitors -- and I think -- I'm sorry. You've already told us. There were people you recognised from Banja Luka who visited. Can you name -- can you tell us who those people were?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were visits on a number of occasions by groups. I recognised some people because I used to go to secondary school in Banja Luka. And through my responsible work that I did, I had contacts with various institutions in Banja Luka before the war, and that is how I met many people. Many used to go to school with me or to university with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause a minute, sir. I think there may be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, go ahead. But keep in mind that in about ten minutes -- eight, ten minutes we -- not we. They need to change the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it may well be that perhaps the answer is then to complete the narrative of the camp and leave the video until after the break -- after -- I mean, when he comes back. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't intending to have another break. I was intending to bring this -- today's session to an end, to a close.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. No. That's what I mean, Your Honour. Rather than waiting till we change the tapes. Judge Draganovic is coming back in two weeks time. And we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Sir. You interrupted -- I interrupted you, rather. You knew these people from Banja Luka. Can you just name some of the people who visited who you knew.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see when they came Prstojevic Dubravko. He went to secondary school with me, and I knew him from there. He would tour the camp two or three times. As far as I was able to learn, he was a Minister for Information or something like that, on behalf of the corps or something. Anyway, with him there would be some journalists. I saw Vlado Slijepcevic, who worked for Serbian radio and television from Bosanska Gradiska. Yes. I know he came from there. I knew him. Then the camp was also visited by Stojan Zupljanin and Nenad Balaban. They were together. I knew them too, and I knew them well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nenad Balaban, what did he do? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I knew at the time was that I think he was head of the military security of the 1st Corps. And Zupljanin was head of the CSB in Banja Luka. Balaban was, I think, in a military uniform, and Zupljanin was in civilian clothes then. They entered the camp, together with the camp commander, Popovic. And I was in the area known as the kitchen or the dining room. It is the area used to stack hay with a cover. And as they were on tour of the camp, I had contacts with them. We stopped -- all three of them stopped to talk to me. I asked them something: "What is this? Why is this? And what's going to happen to us?" And I was given an answer. I also recognised some representatives of the police and the Banja Luka public security centre, Mirko Bojinovic, who was a lawyer and with whom I was on good terms before the war, a good friend. And they had ranks -- senior police ranks. And they were on tour, and I saw them visiting the horse shed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt, Your Honour, but I want to make this request before the tape actually runs out. From here I'm quite certain I can see the piece of paper the witness is referring to now has writing on both sides of it, unless my old eyes deceive me, which I concede is possible. But I think it has writing on both sides, and we have a copy on one side, on one page. And I would request that all of the pages, both pages, that -- if Your Honour wants to inquire if he has used them to refresh his memory in any way, I think that would be appropriate. But if that's the case, I think we're entitled to have all of the papers that he has brought with him, not just one side of one page. And so I make that request specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I see that -- the paper that he has in front of him, that he's showing us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That -- this is this -- the piece of paper. During the last break, I just made some underlining to remind myself. I put "toilet," "bathing," "wake up at 5.00," "stables," "epidemics," "dishes were not washed." So it is on this same piece of paper that I added a few lines. So please copy it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, usher, let me see the paper. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It is the same paper, but it is -- according to me, it is obvious that there are some additions at the bottom of what appears to be the first page, and then there is something written on the back, just four lines, which to me appears to have been written before these three lines were added in the first page. In other words, what you have on the back here seems to have been there before you put these three lines here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I added what is on the back during the break, while I was concentrating, to make sure I didn't forget any details. I put down these brief notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, let's have this photocopied first, please, on both sides. And we'll give it back to the witness immediately. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's also indicated that he has no objection to having the other paper copied too. He has another sheet of paper in his pocket that he had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But I will not ask him to produce that paper if he's not going to make reference to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is -- on this first page you will see that at the bottom, before he added anything, there is a sentence that is half done. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But he said before that he was not going to make reference -- to refresh his memory to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you ask him if he has looked at it any time today to refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will. Have you looked at the second page to refresh your memory during today's testimony? Not before or during the break because that's different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't looked at it, because I didn't need that piece of paper. It was important for me to have the names so I don't make a mistake. And when explaining the conditions in the camp, I just briefly noted down the things I needed to tell you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I fully respect your decision. I wish to inform you, however, that I can read the contents of this document, and this document could have very great importance on this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What importance, Madam Fauveau, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll be glad to explain it to you but not in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Photocopy that document, please. Can we have the second page too? Do you have any objection to having the second page photocopied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So can we have the second page photocopied as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Only let me just have a look to see what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, Ms. Korner, you may continue. We need to change the tape now, unless you want to stop here and resume after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think so -- sir, I I'm sorry. I think, Your Honours, if I can finish the people who came to the camp as a discrete subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll change the tape now and we'll finish immediately after. Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge, you were talking about seeing Zupljanin and Balaban. And you said you spoke to them, saying what was going to happen, and that you got an answer. Who gave you an answer, and what was it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Balaban first asked me, "What are you doing here, and why are you here?" I laughed when I heard this question. I said, "Well, you should know why I'm here." He asked whether any other colleagues were there, any other judges or lawyers. I said that Suad Sabic, a lawyer, was also there. He was a colleague. He was in another camp. And I asked Zupljanin, "What's going to happen to us?" He said, "Everything will be fine. You'll be released. No one will be hurt." And Balaban also told me at the end, "It's better for you to be there than -- it's better for you to be here than in a trench." That was supposed to be a consolation of some kind. And that's what we spoke about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any members -- I'm sorry. Was there one politician in particular who visited and went round all the stables?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, sometime in the summer -- I can't remember the exact date -- one politician did appear. He was from Banja Luka. I think it was Vojo Kupresanin who represented the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And he represented the Crisis Staff of the ARK. He was wearing civilian clothes. I think he had a tie on. He visited all the stables. At the time I was in the kitchen. I was in the stable when he was in my stables, and then I went to the kitchen. He then visited the other stables, so that I could hear what he had to say. He was talking about something -- I can't remember it very well, but he said something to the effect of -- he said we would be released quite soon. "Those who have blood on their hands, they will be held accountable," he said. I saw the people clap. They probably thought that they really would be released. But even then I knew that we wouldn't be released and that we wouldn't return home. I felt sick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- I'm sorry. Do you know if anybody did get released as a direct result of any intervention by any high-ranking politician, or military man, or any sort of eminent figure?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that some individuals had been released, but very few people -- this concerns very few people. I heard that they had given money -- members of their families had given money and they were released. So I know for sure that Nijaz Halilovic was released. He was from Sanski Most. And as I explained earlier on, he was a commander or chief of the Territorial Defence up until the time that the Territorial Defence was dismantled. He wasn't in the Manjaca camp for very long, and I can remember the day when he told me that he was leaving and Branko Basara came to the fetch him. And I think that Branko Basara was a militant and took him away. He was the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade, Branko Basara was when I met --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause for a moment. It's being typed on the screen as Pasara. I think you're saying Basara, "B."

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade, the Sanska Brigade. He had Halilovic in his flat in Banja Luka. He -- Halilovic spent a few days there. That's what Halilovic told me after the war. And he then got him out through Belgrade, through Serbia, and took him to Hungary, because his father worked abroad and put up the money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I also know that certain other individuals were released from the camp, such as Dr. Flat from Kljuc and Miralem, who was a baker. I don't know what his surname is exactly -- and some other individuals. I also saw my president -- the president of the district court in Banja Luka, Jovo Rosic. He also went to the camp. He entered through the gate. He was in civilian clothing. I didn't appear before him because I didn't want to have any contact with him. I don't know why he went there, why he went to the Manjaca camp. He was the president of the high court -- that is to say, of the district court in Banja Luka. I think that he came on two occasions. Perhaps he had certain tasks to carry out. I also saw the judge of the military court of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was he, his name? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just a minute so that I can concentrate. I'll remember the name later on. I saw Radovan Stanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have the name on the list, you can refer to the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I wonder if I can be permitted to lead the list that he gave in his statement. It's probably simplest. And there's no dispute about this. Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it -- Judge, is it right that the judge of the military court in Banja Luka -- there were two -- was somebody called Mirko Adamovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was somebody else called Sveto Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was thinking of them. And above all, I was thinking of the first person, the first person you mentioned he was the judge in the military court. Mirko Adamovic. That's right. He was born in Sanski Most. I saw him. I saw Radovan Stanic, who was a judge -- or rather, the president of the court in Sanski Most. And he was in fact Serbian -- he was a member of the Serbian public security. And he interrogated the inmates in Sanski Most in a police station, in Krings and elsewhere. And he went to Manjaca to interrogate people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any sort of judicial hearing with any of these judges who visited ever held at the camp for any of the prisoners -- or first of all, at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. There were no trials, no hearings. But they probably came to take statements of some kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we stop here, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. That seems an appropriate moment. Your Honour might perhaps care to explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Judge, I suppose you have already been put in the picture. There is going to be a break now, during which you will return home. But then you will be required to come back to The Hague to continue giving your evidence. You will be informed beforehand when you will be required here, and you will receive the usual assistance to be able to come here. And on that occasion -- that will be sometime in May -- I don't have the exact date --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The 13th of May, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The 13th of May you are probably expected to continue your testimony. And on that day, you -- Ms. Korner will continue her direct examination. And following that, during that week, you will be cross-examined by the Defence teams. I thank you for having come here to give evidence, and we will meet again, please God, on the 13th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's probably hardly necessary, but there's every likelihood that Judge Draganovic may run into other witnesses when he returns back to Sanski Most -- potential witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge, I need hardly explain to you the need and the importance that between now and your return to The Hague to continue your evidence, your testimony, you do not discuss these matters with any -- with anyone, particularly persons that may be giving evidence or may have already given evidence here. I think as a judge I don't need to explain to you the importance of this, because I'm sure you understand it. Yes. Anything else from the witness? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The witness may be escorted out of the courtroom. Anything else before we adjourn? So we'll meet on the -- what's the ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 7th of May, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 7th. So we'll meet on the 7th. Have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we're scheduled for 9.00 -- for the morning sessions again starting the 7th of May, unless ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May, I think, is all morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. If I remember well, it is always in the morning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then June we revert to -- not the whole month but the most part of June is in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
